defects.text: Report descriptors >512 bytes aren't served, so the PC's HID driver doesn't load for that interface.
While injecting, even at 10 moves/s, stock reads a 1 kHz mouse whose speed varies only ~290-490 times/s.
If a program closes the port or stops sending while a button or key is held or an input locked, it stays in effect until another program releases it or the box restarts (24/24 tries).
When the PC switches the clone's configuration, stock reconnects the clone instead of relaying the switch to the real device (3/3 tries).

Moves arriving faster than stock takes them (29 or 30 binary moves in one write, ≥10,000 binary moves/s, 8,000 text moves/s, 32 per write every 16 ms, or back to back) are lost, most with no refusal. Every later command then runs one command late until a power cycle (after 29 moves in one write in 1/2 runs, after 8,000 text moves/s in 5/6). 30 characters sent as key presses back to back lose characters.
Neither an injected move nor the real device's remote wakeup wakes a sleeping PC.
Mouse clones declare a 1 ms poll interval even when the mouse declares 2-10 ms (a 125 Hz mouse's clone is polled at 1 kHz). Stock's lower latency below 1 kHz comes from this.

Class requests to the clone sometimes go unanswered: SET_IDLE, SET_PROTOCOL or GET_PROTOCOL in 7/20 tries. In 1/10 port cycles of a PC restart, the clone took 6.1 s to come back: the kernel log shows the PC's HID driver waiting 5 s for such a request.
With the mouse moving, stock refuses moves past ~1,330/s and replies to each refusal (1,326/5,000 arrived at 5,000/s).
When the PC pauses reading an interrupt endpoint, stock drops reports the real device would have kept: 91 counter values skipped in 8,000 reports on each endpoint.
Where the real device replies past wLength (LUFA, STM32's library, V-USB), stock STALLs the request. Standard requests the real device answers sometimes time out on stock (12 over 9 device stacks).
